West of Suez, oil freight costs are falling hard (from all-time highs). The WAF-to-Europe route has more than halved, for example, dropping to its lowest since early September. East of Suez freight remains expensive, however, with the Persian Gulf-to-Far East still >$1m per day.

Saudi Arabia says its critical East-West oil pipeline was attacked again, resulting in a small fire. But Riyadh says the pipeline, the key bypass to avoid the Strait of Hormuz, remains operational despite the attack. 

https://t.co/5F06Mc1c8z

"... Simply put, there is more oil from the Middle East, but there is also more demand for it, notably from renewed buying from China..." -- Jim Burkhard, global head of crude oil research at S&P Global Energy

Oil bears seize control in the futures market

Investors have become increasingly bearish about all parts of the petroleum complex (with the exception of U.S. gasoline) as the United States and Iran have signalled a preference to negotiate rather than resume unrestricted warfare.

Hedge funds and other money managers sold the equivalent of 93 million barrels in the six most important futures and options contracts over the seven days ending on November 3.

Fund managers sold petroleum contracts at the fastest rate for more than ten months since before the U.S. military operations against Venezuela and Iran ...

Chinese crude oil imports rose to a seven-month high in October on a recovery in shipments from the Persian Gulf #oott https://t.co/rYVPiKf4ox

The volume of refined products being loaded within the Persian Gulf is rising, with most of that exiting the Strait of Hormuz and providing some relief to one of the tightest corners of the global oil market nine months into the Iran war.

The region loaded about 3 million barrels a day of distillates including diesel, petrochemical feedstock naphtha and liquefied petroleum gas in October, according to data from ship-tracking and analytics firm Vortexa Ltd. While that’s still only about half of pre-conflict levels, that’s up from a trough in May of about 1 million barrels a day. #oott

Latest Chinese official trade data showed crude oil imports rising to ~9.9 MMbpd in October.

- Highest level since March 
- Up ~1 MMbpd m/m 
- Up ~3  MMbpd from June low
- Still down ~2.5 MMbpd from prewar (Feb) level https://t.co/9i8zcPa9ES

Crude falling nearly $30/bbl over the past ~week makes it much easier for Trump to talk nonchalantly about perpetuating the status quo.

Iran seemingly less so.

But it’s still a game of siege chicken.

No real notable crude price move off this, despite the fact that it would seem to imply that Trump isn't going to go for the latest Qatari-Pakistani proposal that had dragged prices lower today.

Also says "quite unlikely" we see escalation, but that unwind was last week imho.

With ~1400 votes, just more than half see a perpetuation of the messy status quo through the end of 2026.

~25% expect material re-escalation before year-end.

Only ~10% see the war ending via the kind of deal that has tanked crude prices today.

See tweets following this from @AlArabiya_Brk for the details of the latest news to crush crude prices.

Supposedly
- arrangements for the return of IAEA inspectors
- US allowing domestic enrichment up to 3.67% (Iran reportedly agreed)
- Looking for third party country to facilitate reduction of HEU
- US seeking 60% reduction of enriched uranium
- US to release $6-9 bn in Iranian assets if deal made
-  Hormuz would open and blockade would be dropped immediately

We've been here before. Previously fell apart on sequencing and Iran's role in Hormuz, but Iran also now seems to have given up some of the Hormuz ask.
